thesis: Corning reported Q2 2026 on 28 July 2026 and, per CNBC and TheStreet, beat consensus on both revenue and EPS while guiding Q3 revenue below an elevated consensus; Optical Communications — the AI-driven segment carrying the story — grew 32% year over year to $2.07 billion, decelerating from 36% the prior quarter. The stock fell roughly 12-15% that session, its worst day since 2002, and dragged the wider optical group down with it; it fell a further 8% on 18 August. The strongest counter-evidence is that this was a genuine double beat and that Corning has since been named in Amazon and Nvidia fiber agreements — but that does not change the read, because what re-rated the stock was the company's own forward guide and its own disclosed segment deceleration, not the backward-looking print, and neither of those is reversed by design wins that are already inside the guidance. This suggests the multiple was set on an optical growth rate the company is no longer guiding to. No leveraged position taken on a name whose own guidance is the negative catalyst.
invalidation: Corning guides Optical Communications back to accelerating year-over-year growth, or reports a Q3 optical result above the July guide

thesis: Intel priced an upsized public equity offering of roughly 210.5 million shares at $95, taking the raise to about $20 billion from an initially planned $15 billion, and the stock has since traded below that offering price. Benzinga and StocksToTrade tie the August weakness to that dilution plus a broad semiconductor sell-off; FXLeaders reports CPU market share at a three-decade low alongside heavy investment spending. The counter-case is real and I could not settle it: Intel is still up about 149% year to date, so the drawdown may be an unwind of a very large run rather than a change in the recovery thesis, and a funded balance sheet is what the foundry build-out requires. With a completed raise of this size sitting against a share-loss trend, the evidence points in both directions and this run cannot resolve which dominates.
invalidation: Intel trades sustainably back above the $95 offering price on disclosed foundry customer commitments or a reported CPU share stabilisation

thesis: Sandisk reported fiscal Q4 2026 on 5 August 2026: revenue $8.97 billion, up 51% sequentially, with GAAP net income of $6.90 billion ($43.97 diluted GAAP EPS); full-year FY26 revenue $20.25 billion, up 175%. It guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue to $10.30-$10.80 billion with non-GAAP diluted EPS of $44.00-$46.00 — note the guide is stated on a non-GAAP basis while the quarter's headline income is GAAP — and the board added $14 billion to the buyback, taking remaining authorisation to $15.5 billion. Against that, the shares are down roughly 29% over the 60-day window. That gap is the problem, and the explanation I found is not a disclosed fundamental deterioration: reporting from 24/7 Wall St. and Invezz attributes the memory sell-off to weekend reports that Washington may let Apple source DRAM from CXMT and NAND from YMTC, to rising Treasury yields, and to profit-taking after a 653% year-to-date run. So the tape is sentiment- and policy-driven rather than tracking the company's own numbers — which is exactly why this stays unresolved: a China-supply policy shift would be a real change to the pricing cycle these results depend on, and I cannot confirm whether it happens.
invalidation: Reported NAND contract pricing turns down, or the Apple/CXMT-YMTC sourcing reports are confirmed as policy

thesis: Coherent reported fiscal Q4 2026 on 12 August 2026: revenue $2.05 billion, up 33.8% year over year, its seventh consecutive record revenue quarter, with non-GAAP EPS of $1.74 against a consensus around $1.58-$1.62. Both margin figures should be read together — GAAP gross margin was 38.5% versus non-GAAP gross margin of 40.2%, and the $1.74 EPS is the non-GAAP number; I did not read a GAAP EPS in any source this run. Q1 guidance of $2.2-$2.4 billion revenue and $1.85-$2.05 EPS both sat above consensus. The shares are nonetheless down about 24% over the 60-day window, and that contradiction is what I could not settle. The explanation the sources give is positioning, not disclosure: Coherent had already fallen 14% the Monday before the print on pre-earnings profit taking, fell again on the results as a sell-the-news move, and slid roughly 19% in the week to 19 August amid insider selling and the debut of a short ETF on the name. That reads as sentiment-driven rather than a disclosed fundamental deterioration, which leaves the counter-case named and open.
invalidation: Coherent guides below consensus, or reports a sequential decline in AI datacenter optical revenue

thesis: Rocket Lab's Q2 2026 report delivered record revenue of $234.1 million, up 62% year over year and ahead of consensus, with a record backlog of $2.36 billion (up 137%) and over $437 million in new launch contracts — but a wider-than-expected GAAP loss of $0.08 per share. The item that moved the stock is the Neutron timeline: Benzinga reports Stage 1 tank production still aligns with delivering Neutron to the launchpad in Q4 2026, yet the company stopped short of reaffirming a first flight before year-end, and Kalshi traders now put only a 14% probability on a 2026 launch. The evidence is genuinely offsetting and this run could not resolve it: the commercial base is compounding fast and the Iridium acquisition announced in June adds scale, while the single milestone the valuation rests on — roughly 59 times trailing revenue, per The Motley Fool — is the one management declined to reaffirm. This suggests timeline risk rather than demand risk, but not with enough resolution to act.
invalidation: Rocket Lab publicly commits to a dated Neutron first flight, or Neutron slips formally into 2027

thesis: Micron's most recent reported quarter showed revenue up 62% year over year to $8.71 billion with datacenter revenue up 150%, HBM3E sold out through most of 2026, full-year guidance raised to $31.5-$33.5 billion, and capex lifted to roughly $20 billion to add HBM capacity. The stock is nonetheless down about 18% across the 60-day window. The explanation I found is a sector-wide positioning unwind rather than anything Micron disclosed: 24/7 Wall St. and Invezz attribute the late-August memory sell-off to reports that Washington may allow Apple to source DRAM from China's CXMT and NAND from YMTC, to rising Treasury yields pressuring the most extended trade in semiconductors, and to profit-taking after a 255% year-to-date run. Because the driver is a sector-and-policy story that this run cannot settle, the read stays unresolved: HBM's contracted, sold-out nature is a genuine defence against commodity DRAM pricing, but it is not a defence I can confirm holds if Chinese supply is admitted to a major US customer.
invalidation: Micron discloses HBM order cancellations or pricing concessions, or the China memory sourcing reports are confirmed as policy

thesis: Applied Optoelectronics reported Q2 2026 on 6 August 2026: a fifth consecutive record revenue quarter with sales up 86% year over year to $191.9 million, and a return to non-GAAP profitability at adjusted EPS of $0.06 against a $0.02 estimate — that $0.06 is the adjusted figure, and I did not read a GAAP EPS for the quarter in any source this run, so the GAAP result is unconfirmed here. Management guided Q3 revenue to $255-$290 million and adjusted EPS to $0.11-$0.26, and says demand for 800G, 1.6T and 1.8 GHz CATV products exceeds capacity through mid-2027; a reported draft FCC ban on new Chinese optical transceivers is an additional tailwind. The stock surged double digits on the print and has since given it all back, leaving it down about 17% over the 60-day window. The driver of that reversal is not company-specific: the whole optical group de-rated after Corning's 28 July guidance, and AAOI fell with it. A sector-wide re-rating running against the company's own record disclosures is exactly the evidence this run cannot reconcile.
invalidation: AAOI guides Q4 below the Q3 range, or reports 800G/1.6T bookings no longer exceeding capacity

thesis: AST SpaceMobile's Q2 2026 business update on 10 August 2026 missed on both lines as reported by Investing.com: revenue of $31.5 million against a $35.18 million consensus, and an adjusted loss of $0.77 per share against an expected $0.26 loss. Operationally the quarter was stronger than that reads — revenue more than doubled from roughly $15.8 million in Q1, the company has 13 satellites in orbit after launching BlueBird 11, 12 and 13 in early August, backlog is near $1.3 billion, and it reaffirmed 2026 revenue guidance of $150-$200 million. Those two halves do not resolve against each other in this run: reaffirmed full-year guidance of $150-$200 million sits above a first half that the company reported at roughly $47 million combined, so the guide requires a second-half ramp I have no disclosed order-to-revenue schedule to test. Note also that reported cash and equivalents of about $2.7 billion at 30 June is quoted alongside pro forma liquidity above $3.7 billion; I did not read what closes that gap, so I am not treating it as a disclosed raise.
invalidation: AST SpaceMobile trims or withdraws 2026 revenue guidance, or Q3 revenue does not step up materially from $31.5 million

thesis: Nvidia reports fiscal Q2 after the close on 26 August 2026 — tomorrow — with consensus at roughly $92 billion of revenue (about 97% year-over-year growth) and $2.08 EPS. That is a pending catalyst, not a confirmed one, and nothing company-disclosed that I read this run explains the 60-day move; the price action is sector positioning ahead of the print. The counter-case is squarely engaged and unresolved: Yahoo Finance reports the stock has fallen seven straight sessions, its longest losing streak since 2022, on renewed doubts about returns on AI capex, while 58 of 61 analysts still rate it Buy or Strong Buy at what Kiplinger calls a reasonable 25 times forward earnings. Those two readings cannot both be tested until the print lands, and buying into an unresolved binary the day before it resolves is not a thesis. This suggests waiting for the disclosure rather than anticipating it.
invalidation: The 26 August print and accompanying guidance resolve the AI-capex return question in either direction

thesis: Held position. Microsoft closed fiscal 2026 on 29 July 2026 with Q4 revenue of $90.0 billion, up 18% year over year, and operating income of $40.6 billion; Azure revenue passed $100 billion for the first time in a fiscal year, up 41%, and the company guided fiscal Q1 Azure growth to about 45% in constant currency, ahead of expectations. It also ended its revenue-share arrangement with OpenAI, allowing any cloud provider to serve OpenAI models. The strongest counter-evidence is legal, not operational: multiple securities class actions allege Microsoft misled investors about Copilot's commercialisation and about the trade-off between AI capex and Azure capacity, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation in late July into whether Microsoft misled customers on Microsoft 365 pricing and subscription options. Even with those open, the read does not change: both are disclosure and marketing-conduct matters at an early procedural stage with no scheduled ruling, hearing or compliance deadline I could find in the next 90 days, and neither disputes the Azure revenue and growth figures the company itself reported and is guiding above. The 60-day price move tracks that 29 July print rather than running against it, so the tape and the disclosures agree.
invalidation: Azure growth guides below 40% constant currency, or a scheduled ruling or compliance deadline emerges in the securities or CMA matters

thesis: Held position. Dell's most recent reported quarter (fiscal Q1 2027) showed record revenue of $43.8 billion, up 88% year over year, with AI server revenue of $16.1 billion — up 757% — non-GAAP EPS of $4.86 (up 214%; I did not read a GAAP EPS for the quarter in any source this run), and $2.1 billion returned through buybacks and dividends. Fiscal 2027 revenue guidance was raised to $165-$169 billion with roughly $60 billion expected from AI servers. In August, AI cloud startup Volta emerged from stealth naming Dell as technology provider on a $10 billion, 133-megawatt AI factory in Norway. The counter-case is that AI server revenue carries structurally thinner margins than Dell's legacy mix and the stock is up roughly 281% year to date, so much of this is priced. I am not resolving that here, and more importantly Dell reports again on 3 September — an unresolved binary catalyst close enough to reverse this read before the position is likely to be revisited on any horizon that matters. The disclosed trajectory continues to support holding; it does not support treating the read as settled ahead of that print.
invalidation: The 3 September report shows AI server revenue or fiscal 2027 guidance below the raised $165-$169 billion range, or discloses AI-server margin compression

thesis: Held position. Astera Labs reported Q2 2026 on 4 August 2026 with record revenue of $392.4 million, up 104% year over year, beating on both revenue and earnings, and guided fiscal Q3 to $540-$560 million — roughly 40% sequential growth at the midpoint — with non-GAAP EPS of $1.16-$1.21. The stock fell 12% the following session and has kept falling, and is down about 28% across the 60-day window. Trefis frames the drop as 'the rally came first': profit-taking after a large pre-earnings run rather than a disclosed deterioration, with higher operating expense from continued product-roadmap investment and broad competition and macro concerns cited alongside. That framing is the honest one and it leaves the position unresolved rather than reassuring — a move explained by positioning is a move that can continue for as long as positioning unwinds, and the competitive concern in PCIe/CXL connectivity is named in the coverage without being settled by anything the company disclosed. Nothing verified this run says the reason for holding has broken; nothing verified this run resolves why the market disagrees.
invalidation: Astera Labs guides Q4 below the Q3 range, or discloses design-win losses at a major hyperscaler

thesis: Held position, and the strongest signal in this run: up about 42% over the 60-day window and within 0.5% of its 52-week high. What I could verify is regulatory progress on relacorilant — Corcept resubmitted its hypercortisolism NDA to the FDA in May 2026 with the additional data analyses regulators had asked for, and separately the FDA accepted its relacorilant NDA in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer with a target date of 11 July 2026. What I could not verify is the outcome of that 11 July date: no source I read this run states whether the ovarian-cancer application was approved, and one source describes hypercortisolism approval only as anticipated by year-end. I am not inferring an approval from the price move, so the catalyst most likely driving this advance is unconfirmed. The counter-case is engaged and also unsettled: a securities class action alleges the company and executives misled investors about FDA feedback and approval risk in hypercortisolism, and there are reported legal setbacks around Teva's generic Korlym, which is the revenue base the pipeline is funded from — I found no scheduled ruling, hearing or compliance deadline for either in the next 90 days, so neither is flagged, but neither is resolved. Holding remains supported by what is disclosed; the evidence behind the move is not something this run established.
invalidation: A confirmed FDA rejection or further delay on either relacorilant application, or an adverse ruling accelerating generic Korlym entry
